pages.text: AMARAVATI BILL

AMARAVATI BILL



• Parliament passed the Bill on April 2, 2026, recognising
  Amaravati as the sole and permanent capital of Andhra
  Pradesh.

• The Bill amends the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act,
  2014, to provide statutory clarity on the capital issue.

• This ends a decade-long political and legal ambiguity over the
  capital, impacting federal relations and regional development.

AMARAVATI BILL


Bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh –

• The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, bifurcated the
  united state into Telangana and residual Andhra Pradesh.

• Hyderabad was designated as a joint capital for both states for
  a period not exceeding 10 years.

• Key Condition: Andhra Pradesh was required to establish its
  own capital within 10 years (by June 2, 2024).

AMARAVATI BILL


• Hyderabad served as the joint capital for both Telangana and
  Andhra Pradesh until June 2, 2024.

• After this date, Hyderabad became the exclusive capital of
  Telangana, leaving Andhra Pradesh without a capital of its own.

• The problem was that Andhra Pradesh failed to establish a
  permanent capital before the deadline, leading to a legal and
  political vacuum.

AMARAVATI BILL

What is the 2026 Amendment Bill?
• Purpose: To amend Section 5 of the 2014 Act to explicitly name
  Amaravati as the capital.
• Inserts the words “at Amaravati” into Section 5(2).
• Defines Amaravati as including areas notified under the Andhra Pradesh
  Capital Region Development Authority Act, 2014.
• Statutory recognition to Amaravati as the sole capital, retrospectively
  from June 2, 2024.

AMARAVATI BILL


Historical Evolution - The Naidu Era (2014-2019) –

• 2014-2019 (TDP Government): CM N. Chandrababu Naidu
  declared Amaravati as the new capital.

• Launched a greenfield capital project using a Land Pooling Scheme
  (LPS).

• Administration was partially moved out of Hyderabad.

• Outcome: Significant infrastructure development began, but the
  project remained incomplete.

AMARAVATI BILL


• In 2019, the YSRCP government proposed three capitals to
  decentralise development: Visakhapatnam as the executive
  capital, Amaravati as the legislative capital, and Kurnool as
  the judicial capital.

• The reason cited for this proposal was the alleged neglect of
  other regions and grievances over the Land Pooling Scheme.

• This three-capital plan created a major political and legal
  dispute, ultimately leading to the High Court striking it
  down in 2022.

AMARAVATI BILL

• In March 2022, the Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled that the
  state could not shift the capital from Amaravati and questioned
  its legislative competence to reverse the 2014-15 policy
  decision.

• Consequently, the Court struck down the three-capital Act
  as unconstitutional, dealing a major blow to the YSRCP
  government’s decentralisation plan.

• The YSRCP government challenged this judgment in the
  Supreme Court by filing a Special Leave Petition (SLP).

AMARAVATI BILL

• After the NDA returned to power in late 2024, Chief Minister
  Chandrababu Naidu filed an affidavit in the Supreme
  Court affirming his government’s commitment to develop
  Amaravati as the sole capital.

• Consequently, the Special Leave Petition (SLP) filed by the
  previous YSRCP government is now in the process of being
  withdrawn.

• On March 28, 2026, the Andhra Pradesh State Assembly
  passed a resolution seeking statutory recognition for Amaravati
  as the permanent capital.

AMARAVATI BILL

Key features of the Bill –

• The 2026 Bill formally notifies Amaravati as the sole capital
  of Andhra Pradesh, providing statutory recognition to the city.

• It amends the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 to
  remove any ambiguity caused by the earlier three-capital
  proposal.

• This amendment ends the confusion over the status of
  Hyderabad after June 2, 2024, by clearly establishing
  Amaravati as the permanent capital.

AMARAVATI BILL

The Land Pooling Scheme (LPS) –

• Under the Land Pooling Scheme, farmers voluntarily
  contributed their land in exchange for developed, high-value
  plots in the capital region.

• These farmers were to be made partners in development, not
  just compensated for their land.

• However, the YSRCP claims that the interests of these farmers
  remain unaddressed under the current Bill.

AMARAVATI BILL


• The Andhra Pradesh Capital Region Development
  Authority (APCRDA) is the key body that governs capital area
  development in Amaravati.

• The Union government is required to amend the 2014 Act
  only on the basis of a state legislative resolution
  requesting such a change.

• Parliament has final authority under Article 3 of the
  Constitution, which deals with the formation of new states and
  alteration of boundaries.

AMARAVATI BILL


• Section 5 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 did
  not clearly specify the name of Andhra Pradesh’s capital.

• The three-capital proposal introduced by the YSRCP government
  created legal ambiguity and policy confusion regarding the
  capital.

• The 2026 Amendment ensures clarity, stability, and continuity in
  governance by providing explicit statutory recognition to
  Amaravati.

AMARAVATI BILL


Important Developments - Timeline (2024-2026) –

June 2, 2024: Joint capital arrangement with Hyderabad ends.

Late 2024: NDA government returns; files affidavit supporting
Amaravati.

March 28, 2026: State Assembly passes resolution.

April 2, 2026: Parliament passes the Amendment Bill.

AMARAVATI BILL


• The Bill was passed with broad political consensus, with even
  the principal Opposition party, the Congress, extending its
  support.

• The BJP, TDP, Congress, and other regional parties voted in
  favour of the Bill.

• Only the YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) opposed the Bill,
  citing unaddressed farmer grievances under the Land Pooling
  Scheme.

AMARAVATI BILL


• The YSRCP stated that it was not opposing the capital itself but
  the “form” of the Bill, demanding a clear timeline for
  compensating farmers under the Land Pooling Scheme.

• The party argued that the Bill ignores unfulfilled promises
  made to farmers who had parted with their land for the capital
  project.

• YSRCP MP P.V. Midhun Reddy further stated that farmer
  compensation should be incorporated into the Bill itself.

AMARAVATI BILL


• The core concern is that over 30,000 farmers contributed
  their land under the Land Pooling Scheme (LPS) for the
  development of Amaravati.

• Many of these farmers have still not received the promised
  developed plots or adequate compensation for their land.

• The Bill’s complete silence on this issue remains a major
  criticism from the YSRCP, which has repeatedly raised the matter.

AMARAVATI BILL


• The estimated cost of developing Amaravati is over ₹1 lakh
  crore for the initial phases alone.

• The state’s finances are already strained, and it relies heavily on
  central assistance to fund the capital project.

• There is a clear need for private investment and public-
  private partnership (PPP) models to meet the financial
  requirements.

AMARAVATI BILL

• Proponents of the three-capital argument claimed it would
  prevent regional imbalance and the over-concentration of
  resources in a single city.

• Critics argue that making Amaravati the sole capital may lead to
  the neglect of other regions such as Rayalaseema (Kurnool)
  and the coastal areas around Visakhapatnam.

• This reveals a fundamental tension between efficiency, which
  favours a single capital, and equity, which supports
  decentralisation of development.

AMARAVATI BILL

Centre-State Relations –

• Constitutional Dimension: Under Article 3, Parliament has
  power to alter state boundaries and names.

• However, capital location is generally a state subject under
  Schedule 7.

• The amendment shows that central legislation can override
  state executive action on capital.

AMARAVATI BILL


• Andhra Pradesh has long demanded Special Category Status
  (SCS) to compensate for the loss of Hyderabad as its
  capital.

• The central government has not granted SCS but has instead
  offered special financial packages to the state.

• The statutory recognition of Amaravati as the sole capital may be
  linked to broader development assurances provided to the state.

AMARAVATI BILL

Conclusion –

• The 2026 Amendment ends a decade of legal uncertainty and
  reaffirms the primacy of statutory clarity in federal
  governance.

• However, the exclusion of farmer compensation from the Bill
  remains a significant oversight.

• The challenge ahead is to balance legal finality with social
  justice and regional equity.

Myanmar President

• Recently, Myanmar’s coup leader has won a parliamentary
vote to become the ⁠country’s president, formalising his grip on
political power in the war-torn nation five years after he ousted
an elected government.

• Senior General Min Aung Hlaing won 429 out of the 584
votes cast by MPs in the country’s pro-military parliament.

• The transition from top general to civilian president follows a
lopsided election in December and January that was won in a
landslide by an army-backed party.

Myanmar President

About Myanmar –

• Myanmar (officially the Republic of the Union of Myanmar,
also called Burma) is a country in Southeast Asia and the
largest by area in Mainland Southeast Asia, bordering China,
India, Thailand, Bangladesh, and Laos.

• The capital is Naypyidaw, while Yangon (formerly Rangoon)
is the largest city and main commercial centre.

• The population is about 55–57 million, comprising over 135
officially recognised ethnic groups.

Myanmar President


• Buddhism is the dominant religion (around 88%), with
Christian and Muslim minorities.

• The official language of the country is Burmese.

• The country was known as Burma in English until 1989. In
1989, the military government changed the name to Myanmar,
calling Burma a colonial-era term linked mainly to the Burman
ethnic group.

Myanmar President


• The United Nations and many international bodies use
Myanmar, while countries such as the United States continue
using Burma as a political protest.

• Myanmar (Burma) remained under British colonial rule
from 1824 to 1948. From 1886 to 1937, Burma was
governed as a province of British India.

• In 1937, Britain separated Burma from India, making it a
Crown Colony until independence in 1948.

Myanmar President


Journey of Myanmar President –

• Under the 2008 Constitution, Myanmar has three levels of
government: the Union Government (central authority),
Regions and States with their own governments headed by a
Chief Minister, and Self-Administered Divisions/Zones
governed by a Leading Body with executive powers.

• Elections are held for three legislative levels: the national
parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw)—comprising the House of
Representatives (Pyithu Hluttaw) and House of
Nationalities (Amyotha Hluttaw)—and the 14
Region/State Assemblies.

Myanmar President


• Although elections occurred during British rule (notably 1922,
1925, 1928, 1932, 1936), the focus begins with elections in
independent Burma.

• April 1947 elections were held to form a Constituent
Assembly ahead of independence in 1948; the Karen
National Union and most of the Communist Party of Burma
(CPB) boycotted.

• The Constitution of the Union of Burma was approved in
September 1947; U Nu became Prime Minister after Aung
San’s death.

Myanmar President



• In the 1956 elections, held in phases due to conflict, AFPFL
retained power but with a reduced majority; later in June 1958,
the party split into “Clean” AFPFL (U Nu) and “Stable” AFPFL
(U Kyaw Nyein, U Ba Swe).

• In December 1958, General Ne Win seized power as head
of a military caretaker government, becoming interim Prime
Minister.

• On 2 March 1962, Ne Win staged a coup, establishing a
military authoritarian regime that ruled for decades.

Myanmar President


• A 1973 constitutional referendum created a one-party
state; the BSPP won all seats in 1974, and again in 1978,
1981, and 1985, with reported turnouts above 90%.

• In the 27 May 1990 election, the first multiparty poll since
1960, the Aung San Suu kyi’s National League for
Democracy (NLD) won 392 of 492 seats, but the military
refused to recognise the results and continued ruling until 2011.

• A constitutional referendum on 10 May 2008 approved a
new constitution amid controversy following Cyclone Nargis; it
reserved 25% of legislative seats for the military and barred
leaders with foreign family ties from the presidency.

Myanmar President


• The 7 November 2010 election, held under the 2008
Constitution, was boycotted by the NLD; the military-backed
USDP won most seats.

• Later both 2015 and 2020 elections gave the NLD a landslide
victory.

• Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power,
citing unsubstantiated fraud allegations in the 2020 elections won
by Aung San Suu Kyi’s NLD.

Myanmar President


• On 1 February 2021, the military led by Senior General Min
Aung Hlaing staged a coup, establishing the State
Administration Council and overturning the elected
government.

• Under the 2008 constitution, elections must be held within six
months of lifting the state of emergency, but the military
government has delayed it due to ongoing conflicts.

Myanmar President


What has been the manner of election?

• Myanmar’s elections have historically been conducted
through direct popular voting using the First-Past-The-Post
(FPTP) system, though the framework has changed under
different constitutional arrangements.

• From 1948 to 2020, most elections followed FPTP, where the
candidate with the highest votes in a single-member
constituency wins, a system that favoured large parties and
enabled landslide victories for the National League for
Democracy (NLD) in 2015 and 2020.

Myanmar President



• Presidential Myanmar President are indirect, and citizens
do not vote directly for the President.

• Three groups—the elected Lower House members, elected
Upper House members, and the appointed military bloc—
each nominate one vice-presidential candidate.

• The combined parliament votes on the three nominees; the
top vote-getter becomes President, while the other two become
Vice-Presidents.

Myanmar President


• Voter turnout was historically high in credible elections,
reaching around 70% in 2015 and 2020.

• While earlier elections used paper ballots, the most recent
elections introduced Myanmar Electronic Voting Machines
(MEVMs), which do not allow write-in candidates or
spoiled ballots, raising transparency concerns.

Myanmar President


How were the elections being conducted now?

• The election were being held in a three-phase schedule due to the
ongoing civil war and were conducted by the military-backed Union
Solidarity and Development Party (USDP).

➢ The USDP is an ultranationalist, pro-military political party in
  Myanmar, acting as the main military-aligned proxy against the
  National League for Democracy.
➢ Formed in 2010 by General Thein Sein, it acts as a strategic
  instrument of the military junta, controlling the government and
  legislature after winning recent military-run polls.

Myanmar President


• A total of 57 political parties are officially registered to
participate in the elections.

• Only 6–8 parties are contesting nationwide, while about 51
parties are regional or ethnic-based.

• The USDP is the only party capable of contesting almost all
seats due to direct military backing and resources.

Myanmar President


• Major opposition parties, including the National League for
Democracy (NLD) and Shan Nationalities League for
Democracy (SNLD), were dissolved in 2023 for refusing to
comply with new junta-imposed election laws.

• The junta replaced the earlier First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) system
with a Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP) system, aimed at
preventing landslide victories like those in 2015 and 2020.

• The Pyithu Hluttaw (Lower House) continues to elect 330
members through FPTP, while the Amyotha Hluttaw (Upper
House) uses a proportional representation system blended
with FPTP.

Myanmar President


• Regardless of election outcomes, 25% of seats in all
legislatures (110 lower house seats and 56 upper house
seats) remain reserved for military appointees, giving the
junta a permanent veto over constitutional amendments.

• For the first time, voting is being conducted using the
Myanmar Electronic Voting Machine (MEVM) at polling
stations.

Myanmar President


The results -

• Myanmar’s parliament has appointed military chief Min Aung
Hlaing as president.

• He secured 429 of 584 votes, highlighting the strong influence
of military-aligned and appointed members in parliament.

• Hlaing was elected as the 11th President of Myanmar by the
military-dominated parliament, formalising his grip on the
country's political apparatus for the next five years.

Myanmar President



• Min Aung Hlaing was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the
Defence Services of Myanmar's armed forces, known as the
Tatmadaw, in 2011.

• In 2017, when Aung San Suu Kyi was the "de facto" head of
government, as Min Aung Hlaing led Junta carried out a genocide
against Rohingyas.

• He rose to global prominence following the 2021 coup. The
military-aligned Union Solidarity and Development Party won
more than 80% of seats.

Myanmar President


Why is it being called a sham?

• The 2025–2026 Myanmar general election is widely
described as a “sham” and a “theatre of the absurd” by
bodies including the United Nations, as it is viewed as an
attempt by the military junta to create a façade of legitimacy
while retaining full control.

• The most popular political force, the National League for
Democracy (NLD), along with 39 other parties, was officially
dissolved for refusing to comply with restrictive new party
registration laws.

Myanmar President


• Key democratic leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remain
imprisoned on what critics term politically motivated and
frivolous charges, effectively excluding them from the political
process.

• In mid-2025, the junta enacted severe “election protection”
laws that criminalise criticism of the electoral process, with
penalties ranging from decades in prison to the death
sentence.

• Reports indicate that young activists have already received
sentences of nearly 50 years’ imprisonment merely for
displaying anti-election posters.

Myanmar President


• The electoral framework has been altered through a shift to
Proportional Representation (PR) in the upper house, replacing
first-past-the-post, a move analysts say is intended to fragment
opposition votes and weaken any challenge to the USDP.

• Under the 2008 Constitution, the military is guaranteed 25% of
all parliamentary seats, regardless of election outcomes, granting
the junta a permanent veto over constitutional amendments.

• The United Nations has reported cases of coercion, including
civilians and internally displaced persons being threatened with
airstrikes or property confiscation if they failed to participate in
voting.

Myanmar President


• Ongoing civil war has led to voting being cancelled in at least
65 townships, effectively disenfranchising millions in areas
beyond junta control.

• The use of electronic-only voting machines alongside
expanded biometric tracking and AI-based surveillance has
raised concerns that the election is being used to monitor and
repress political dissent.

• While China, Russia, and Belarus have endorsed the process
by sending observers, the European Union, United States,
and several major ASEAN members have refused to recognise
the election results.

Myanmar President


India- Myanmar border –

• The border between India and Myanmar was demarcated by the
British in 1826.

• India and Myanmar established diplomatic relations in 1951,
shortly after Myanmar's independence in 1948.

• There are around 2 million people of Indian origin in Myanmar,
reflecting strong cultural and historical connections.

Myanmar President


• India shares a 1,643-kilometer border with Myanmar. This
border passes through Arunachal Pradesh (520 km),
Nagaland (215 km), Manipur (398 km) and Mizoram (510
km).

• Out of 1,643 km, demarcation of 1,472 km has been
completed. India is currently in the process of fencing the border
and end the Free Movement Regime (FMR) to enhance national
security.
